title: Gateless Barrier, Case 20: Sung-Yuan's Person of Great Strength
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Gateless Barrier Case 20, in which Master Sungyuan asks why a person of great strength can't lift a leg. Nomon reads the Wikipedia entry on Jiriki (self-power) and Tairiki (other power), then asks who directs the mind in zazen, recalling a philosopher and a neuroscientist debating whether anyone can notice wandering and bring the mind back, and an Eddie Murphy movie where a tiny alien drives a human robot. Nomon then reads Sandy Boucher's Tricycle essay about her partner Martha's painful recovery from knee surgery, when a wrong turn in Oakland leads Sandy to a lit shrine of Guan Yin, and a Vietnamese woman there greets Sandy with a hug.

sentences.text: It would reveal more meaning, more layers of understanding for you, so I don't know which of those is true.
This master, Master Sungyuan, I don't know a lot about otherwise.
He was in the Lin Chi, or in Japanese Rinzai line.
He died in 1202, right after Dogen was born.
The stories say he always used questions like this; he'd get up and ask a question.
Here, the two questions in the story are: why can't the person of great strength lift up a leg?
And why doesn't he use his tongue when speaking?
The commentaries say there was usually a third question, which is: why is it that someone of great realization does not cut off the vermillion thread?
Someone of great realization, why don't they cut off the vermillion thread?
So I thought we'd focus on the first question; the one is probably plenty for us.
Why can't a person of great strength lift up a leg?
There's a lot here—something about abilities, something about powers, great strength.
So what are your abilities and powers?
There's something also about limitations: can't lift a leg.
We all also have many limitations.
I mean, there's something here too about assumptions.
We always think that something should be true because something else is true, because that's how it usually is, or we think it usually is.
So we think, if I have great strength, I should be able to lift up my leg.
I should be able to do it.

This made me think of one of the great debates in Japanese religion, as I understand it, which is a debate about whether spiritual power and spiritual progress is really about our own doing or about some other power—it's our practice about self-power or other power.
Back in the day, I used to hear various Dharma talks about this, and this is an area where the Japanese terms sound really cool and they persist even though we don't speak Japanese.
So these two topics here are Jiriki and Tairiki.
Jiriki is self-power, and Tairiki is other power.
Or Tairiki, not Tairiki, Tairiki.
I was trying to remember what those mean exactly, so I looked on Wikipedia where all these things are.
They didn't have Wikipedia when I was hearing these talks, and the Wikipedia article is actually just three paragraphs, so I think it's worth reading.
This is worth considering, you know.
I think we have a lot of assumptions about this, and different people have different assumptions.
Here's the article: Jiriki is the Japanese Buddhist term for self-power, the ability to achieve liberation or enlightenment through one's own efforts.
Jiriki and Tairiki are two terms in Japanese Buddhist schools that classify how one becomes spiritually enlightened.
Jiriki is very much urgent practice in Zen Buddhism, so maybe that's us; we're doing Zazen.
And Tairiki is stressed in Pure Land Buddhism, where it often refers to the power of Amitabha Buddha.
The two terms describe strands of practice that followers of every religion throughout the world develop and debate.

In most religions, you find popular expressions of faith which rely on the worship of external powers, such as an idol of some kind that's expected to bestow favor after being given offerings of faith from a believer.

Some believers of Pure Land Buddhism accept that through faith and reliance on Amitabha Buddha one will be led to enlightenment, just as some Western Christians believe that asking Jesus to cleanse one's sins will lead to attainment of such a desire.
So says the author of this, these are examples of Tairiki, reliance on a power outside oneself for salvation.
Jiriki is experiencing truth for oneself and not merely accepting the testimony of another.
An example of Jiriki in Buddhism is the practice of meditation.
In meditation, one observes the body, often by following the breath, and contemplates the principles like impermanence and dependent arising or emptiness.
Such principles are formally discussed in the Buddhist scriptures, but Jiriki implies experiencing them for oneself.
According to this little article, we're a self-power school, which is maybe why people come here because that kind of fits a sort of Western scientific frame: we should do it ourselves.
And meditation has a scientific evidence base, so if I do the meditation, I'll be better, I'll feel better, which makes some sense.
There's something about all those eyes in there that feel problematic, don't they?
Like, I want this, I'll get that, I'll feel better, I'll do meditation—me, me, me, me, me.
So maybe this question from Master Songyun is a criticism of this.
He's a Zen teacher saying, why can't a person of great strength lift up a leg?
Kind of like, why can't a person with great meditation get enlightened?
What's wrong with that guy?
It's me saying that it's a mistake.
Maybe the pediatrics is wrong, he realized thousands of years ago.
It's a mistake to think this is something I do, something I have power to do.
I'm strong, shouldn't I be able to do what I want?
Maybe I'm strong in my body, maybe I'm strong in my mind, maybe I'm a good talker, maybe I'm well-educated.
I'm well-educated; there are certain things I should get to do and other things I should not have to do.
But, you know, and then it gets frustrating, right?
Then it seems like the world doesn't always work that way.
In this case, I'm strong, how come I can't lift my leg?
But I think more common for us is something like, if I'm so capable and smart, why do I keep doing all these dumb things?
Then, you know, we sit down and we do zazen, we do meditation, and you see these simple instructions.
I hope we give nice, simple instructions.
I hope they were nice and simple: be present, follow your breath, notice when your mind wanders, bring it back.
You'll gradually increase in concentration.
But we imply that you can do this somehow; you're the one directing your mind.
But you don't have to sit very long to wonder about that.
Is that really true?
It doesn't seem like I'm directing my mind that well; the mind's going all over the place.
Maybe you think everybody else must be doing it, so do we really meditate with our own self-power?
I watched this debate between a philosopher and a neuroscientist once about this idea, which we say all the time in here.
After you notice your mind has wandered, and you can do something, and the philosopher said, how do you know that's possible?
Because when your mind is wandering, you wouldn't be there to notice that it was wandering.
You would be wandering, right?
Maybe you have all these other minds available.
Maybe it's that you just happened to come back from your wandering, and then you said, oh, I must have been wandering, but you're already back.
So do you really have this capacity of bringing the mind back, or does it come back and then you notice it came back?
The neuroscientist said, oh, no, no, we're very sure that you can do that.
We put people in the lab and we tell them stuff, and we watch the scans, but it was inconclusive.
So we think we're meditating, but maybe meditation is meditating us, and we're just along for the ride taking credit, basically.
And who is this meditation?
Maybe this is actually the workings of Tairiki, of other power, something happening beyond this idea of me as if I was this little guy in a control booth.
I can't remember the name of it, but there was this great movie with Eddie Murphy where he was an alien, and a tiny little alien, like this big.
And what they figured out how to infiltrate New York, it's always New York, right, is to make these enormous human robots, and he was inside driving.
So he's like inside this human robot driving.
I think, oh, that's kind of the self, isn't it?
No, do this, do that.
But the body wasn't always cooperating.
He had trouble with the controls, so it was pretty funny.
I forget what that was called.
It was a long time ago, big impression on me, Eddie Murphy there.
But anyway, who's really doing the work here?
Who's really making things happen?
Is it us?
Is it through our conscious control, or is there something bigger at work?

So think about the last time you got really upset, for instance, really bent out of shape about something, made something awful happen that you didn't want to happen, or you couldn't get something you wanted, or something like this.
What really helps, then?
What really helps?
Probably some self-power helps.
Maybe you did something, you went on a walk, or you called a friend.
But maybe there's something bigger that helps, too.
Something changes over time, right?
Is it really you that calms down?
Does something else help you calm down?
This one made me think of a story that I saw recently in Tricycle magazine, so I'll show you that.
It's a good story.
An idea of this is a story to help us kind of get a sense of this self-power and other power: are we the ones that figure everything out?
Is there something else at play?
This little article called Meeting the Friend She Always Knew.
There's a little story.
This is by Sandy Belcher, American Apostolic Teacher.
Some experiences take us into a realm rarely visited except in nightmares.
And there I am, dragged through the scenes that slip out of their contours to coalesce into entirely new and terrifying aspect.
What began as a routine procedure has morphed into a grand, weenal horror turn, in which I keep trying to believe in what's happening without any context or rationale to guide me.
I find myself in this condition for almost a month this autumn.
Martha, my partner, has gone in for double knee replacement.
Brave, yes, but nothing we can't handle.
We researched, prepared, set up the reckless equipment, invited friends to visit and help with the recuperation.
She was to come home the day after the surgery.
Instead, like a cable car careening off its tracks, we hurtle into unknown territory.
Terrified passengers are holding on for the rest of their life, because Martha awakes from her anesthesia to intense, unexpected pain like electric shocks radiating down her thighs.
The picture tilts, predictability slips away, and the mass becomes a desperate attempt to control the shocks by doctors and nurses who have no clue what the cause might be.
Addled by oxytocin, Martha cannot control her reaction to the pain, and I enter this madness with her.
Most excruciating for me is the absence of the personality I know and love.
Instead, I am confronted by an oddly familiar yet impossible stranger.
Helpless, pumped up with adrenaline, and soon exhausted, I respond mechanically to what is required of me.
Entering into the 4 a.m. and treating phone call, the drug-fueled argument, the sight of my beloved writhing in an uncontrollable pain on a hospital bed, this situation goes on for days on end.
I spend several good hours with another dreaded crash into the unbelievable pain.
You may ask how my many years of Buddhist practice could be called upon in this emergency.
I experience only the necessity to arrive in the moment, help if I can, stand by if I can't.
And then, despite myself, I am guided to a place of refuge.
The rehabilitation center where Martha lives is situated in a mixed neighborhood in Oakland, hilly streets of old frame dwellings and various states of repair or decrepitude.
Some street trash, some potholes, some well-tended houses.
The rehab employees impress upon me their warning that this is not a safe neighborhood to wander around in at night.
So some nights I pull out my senior taxi script for a ride home.
But this night I'm driving.
In a few blocks from the rehab, I take a wrong turn.
Now I'm entering a cul-de-sac of well-maintained houses when down at the end I see a blaze of light.
What could this be?
I drive slowly towards it and gradually make out a structure built on the sidewalk, like three little houses or three show windows open to the street.
When I pull up I realize this is a shrine.
I park to get out and come closer.

Behind a protective grate in each of the three enclosures, one featuring a Buddha statue whose neon halo rotates slowly, but my eyes are drawn to the other figures: two large statues of Guan Yin, the Bodhisattva of compassion.
Here she is seated, peaceful, gazing out of the neighborhood, the goddess I have been researching and encountering in my 35 years of Buddhist practice, sitting right here in Oakland.
In vases of flowers, real ones, not plastic, with music softly playing, the lights offer up this presence from the surrounding darkness.
I'm astonished, grateful, and puzzled that I seem to have had no foreknowledge of the existence of this shrine, but not surprised by the figure of Guan Yin.
After all these years of chanting to and honoring this Bodhisattva, by now I find her as familiar as an old friend, the reality of her interwoven into my psyche.
I breathe in my tight chest penetrating by the coolness radiating from Buddha's hint of a smile, Guan Yin's lowered eyelids, an expression of deep concentration.
My experience these days is so very dark and overheated, a kind of fetid scrabbling to stay afloat.
But here all is spacious and light.
I feel myself relaxing.
The next day I bring this experience as a gift to Martha.

She is pleased and she takes this expansive feeling with her into the struggle that she has now accepted much better: to wean herself from the opioid that is causing her such disorientation while not actually lessening her thigh pain.
Two afternoons later when I drive to the shrine again, I see that the grating has pushed back.
Flesh flowers rest on three altars.
A tray of red apples have been placed at Buddha's feet.
Incense sticks send out their fragrant smoke.
Guan Yin sits contained and peaceful.
And now I see a small woman with Asian features dressed in black pajamas sweeping the sidewalk next to the shrine.
Noticing my presence, she puts her broom down and comes to see me.
She opens her arms saying, "Oh, I'm so glad to see you again," and reaches up to unfold me in a warm hug.
In her embrace I feel received and am not at all surprised that she somehow knows of the ordeal I am caught in.

As I set off her home, despite my long held secular mindset, despite all the skepticism I normally cultivate about mystical occurrences, religious visitations, divine beings—that stuff for someone else to experience but not for me.
As I drive through the streets of Oakland, I know without a doubt that I have been greeted by, held by, blessed by Guan Yin herself, the living embodiment of the Bodhisattva.
The recognition brings an explosion of light in my chest.
I breathe deeply, letting go of the tension in my shoulders.
And that night I go to sleep feeling opened and at peace for the first time in many weeks.
My next visit to the shrine, I notice that the lettering across the front is Vietnamese.
And the woman wearing the grey pants on top and the top of a monk is seated in the center section of the shrine in a small round pillow.
She faces the altar chanting as she glances down at a book propped before her.
I try not to disturb her, but she notices me and gets up to hug me.
When I ask, she tells me yes, she is Vietnamese.
And now I have a slight ripple of remembrance: didn't I read about this shrine years ago but never was able to find it?
Never mind.
I'm just glad to be in her presence.
I think I'll stop there.
The rest is more about her and her partner, that's expecting she's okay.
So we work hard, right?
We try our best.
We put all our energy in.
We try to help ourselves and our friends.
And sometimes it's not quite enough, right?
Jiriki, Jiriki doesn't quite get us all the way there—self-power.
And somehow if we're open to it, maybe Jiriki, other power, is here too.
So that's my little take on this bizarre question about lifting legs: why can't a person of great strength lift a leg?
We can't always do it all ourselves.
If you're listening.
